title: What AML checks are required for business customers?
summary: Learn the statutory anti-money laundering (AML) checks required for commercial customers under the Bank Secrecy Act, CDD Rule, and FinCEN standards.
body_markdown:
Commercial anti-money laundering compliance in the United States derives from the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), codified at 31 U.S.C. Section 5311 et seq., as amended by Title III of the USA PATRIOT Act and the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020. Under administrative regulations enforced by the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), a bureau of the U.S. Department of the Treasury, covered financial institutions must implement risk-based controls to prevent commercial accounts from being exploited for money laundering, terrorist financing, or sanctions evasion.


Unlike consumer compliance programs that evaluate a single individual applicant, commercial AML compliance evaluates multi-layered legal entities. Financial institutions, including depository banks, registered broker-dealers, futures commission merchants, and mutual funds, cannot rely solely on unverified corporate assertions. Under the FFIEC Customer Identification Program guidance, covered organizations must establish written procedures to verify the identity of the customer to the extent reasonable and practicable.


Legal Entity Customer Identification Program (CIP): Mandated under 31 C.F.R. Section 1020.220, banks must obtain an applicant's legal business name, physical operating address, and taxpayer identification number (typically an EIN). The CIP rule gives institutions flexibility to use documentary methods, non-documentary verification methods (such as querying public registries or credit bureaus), or a combination of both to form a reasonable belief that they know the true identity of the customer.


Beneficial Ownership Identification and Verification (CDD Rule): Enforced under 31 C.F.R. Section 1010.230 (CDD Final Rule), covered institutions must identify and verify the natural persons behind legal entity customers across two mandatory prongs: the ownership prong (identifying each natural person who directly or indirectly owns 25 percent or more of equity) and the control prong (identifying at least one natural person holding significant managerial responsibility to control the entity).


Sanctions and Watchlist Screening: Regulations administered by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) prohibit U.S. persons and financial institutions from transacting with sanctioned individuals, entities, or jurisdictions. While OFAC regulations do not prescribe a specific screening checklist or mandate scanning every account opening automatically, institutions face strict liability for transactions involving blocked persons. Consequently, institutions implement automated screening across legal entity names, DBAs, and beneficial owners to comply with OFAC sanctions programs.


Customer Due Diligence and Ongoing Transaction Monitoring: Under 31 C.F.R. Section 1020.320, institutions must establish a customer risk profile based on the nature and purpose of the customer relationship and conduct ongoing monitoring to identify and report suspicious transactions on a risk basis.
